claims.text: The starting coating has a dual-phase FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy microstructure with heterogeneous grain and phase boundaries.
A controlled thermal treatment or cooling-rate change can increase or modify FCC/BCC phase-boundary density and structure.
Increasing phase-boundary density or modifying FCC/BCC interface character will enhance creep resistance.
Stress and temperature significantly influence creep behavior in high-entropy alloys or superalloys.
Creep can involve atomic diffusion, dislocation nucleation, and dislocation motion, with the dominant mechanism changing with applied stress.
Microstructural factors such as phase lattice misfit and phase volume fraction can critically affect creep resistance.
Modified FCC/BCC phase boundaries act as barriers to dislocation nucleation.
Modified FCC/BCC phase boundaries act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Multiscale simulations predict that tailored FCC/BCC interfaces increase the local threshold stress for dislocation movement.
Dislocation behavior, including cross-slip, can influence creep resistance in high-entropy alloys.
Processed coatings with enhanced phase-boundary characteristics will have lower steady-state creep rates than as-deposited coatings.
Processed coatings will exhibit localized dislocation pile-ups at or near modified FCC/BCC interfaces.
The proposed beneficial effect is expected in stress and temperature regimes where dislocation-mediated and diffusion-assisted creep are active.
The magnitude of creep-rate reduction may depend on the type of phase-boundary modification and the microstructural scale.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing an otherwise identical post-treated coating against an as-deposited control under matched sustained stress and temperature.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant creep-rate reduction, or failure to observe corresponding dislocation blocking, would falsify the stated combined performance-and-mechanism hypothesis.
